arXiv:2604.24693v1 [cs.CL] 27 Apr 2026

Contextual Linear Activation Steering of Language Models

Brandon Hsu1 Daniel Beaglehole1 Adityanarayanan Radhakrishnan2,3 Mikhail Belkin1
1UC San Diego, 2 MIT, 3 Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard
Abstract

Linear activation steering is a powerful approach for eliciting the capabilities of large language models and specializing their behavior using limited labeled data. While effective, existing methods often apply a fixed steering strength to all tokens, resulting in inconsistent steering quality across diverse input prompts. In this work, we introduce Contextual Linear Activation Steering (CLAS), a method that dynamically adapts linear activation steering to context-dependent steering strengths. Across eleven steering benchmarks and four model families, it consistently outperforms standard linear activation steering and matches or exceeds the performance of ReFT and LoRA in settings with limited labeled data. We therefore propose CLAS as a scalable, interpretable, and accurate method for specializing and steering large language models.11 1 Code available at: https://github.com/bhdsc/CLAS.

1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) [9, 39] exhibit powerful capabilities, yet the underlying mechanisms that give rise to these capabilities remain largely opaque. A promising lens for mechanistic understanding is provided by the linear representation hypothesis [25, 24, 28, 26, 19, 27], a key empirical observation positing that semantic concepts in LLMs, which form the basis of their capabilities, are represented as fixed linear directions within their activation spaces. A common approach for identifying such concepts is probing [3, 2, 17, 7, 33, 8], wherein a dataset of prompts and concept labels is used to train a model on the internal activations of an LLM to measure the amount of concept-specific information encoded in those activations. Beyond their use in concept detection, linear directions extracted from these probes can also enable linear activation steering (LAS) [21, 34, 40, 5, 6], where model generations are steered toward concept-specific behavior by adding these directions back into the activations during inference. In particular, let 𝒉ℓ,t∈ℝk\bm{h}_{\ell,t}\in\mathbb{R}^{k} denote the activation at the output of the ℓ\ell-th transformer block22 2 Here, LLMs are described as autoregressive models composed of transformer blocks, where each block consists of layer normalization, self-attention, MLPs, and residual connections [36]. and the tt-th token position of an LLM, and let 𝒅ℓ∈ℝk\bm{d}_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{k} be a unit-norm steering vector extracted from a probe trained on the output of block ℓ\ell. LAS involves replacing 𝒉ℓ,t\bm{h}_{\ell,t} during inference with 𝒉~ℓ,t=𝒉ℓ,t+α​𝒅ℓ\tilde{\bm{h}}_{\ell,t}=\bm{h}_{\ell,t}+\alpha\bm{d}_{\ell}, where α∈ℝ\alpha\in\mathbb{R} is a scalar steering coefficient. This simple yet general approach has been used to induce and control numerous latent capabilities in LLMs such as sentiment control [34], reasoning [4], and persona adoption [6], among many others [5].

While LAS is remarkably simple and effective, selecting steering coefficients that perform well across diverse prompts remains a key bottleneck in practice [5]. This is because the steering coefficient α\alpha is often tuned via an expensive grid search over coefficient values, requiring human or LLM evaluations of the generated outputs to select the best value [34, 21, 40, 30, 20, 35, 11, 6, 13]. Importantly, a more fundamental limitation is that these coefficients are context-independent: a fixed scalar is applied uniformly to all inputs, ignoring variations in prompt or context, and frequently to all blocks of the model [5, 6]. This limitation leads to systematic under- or over-steering, making current approaches brittle with respect to the choice of α\alpha and limiting real-world deployment, where α\alpha cannot be tuned per-prompt or on-the-fly.

To address these limitations, we introduce Contextual Linear Activation Steering (CLAS), which modulates the amount of steering based on the input context and the specific model block using a learned sensing vector 𝒄ℓ∈ℝk+1\bm{c}_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{k+1}. This sensing vector enables context-dependent activation steering: 𝒉~ℓ,t=𝒉ℓ,t+(𝒄ℓ⋅[𝒉ℓ,t​ 1])​𝒅ℓ\tilde{\bm{h}}_{\ell,t}=\bm{h}_{\ell,t}+(\bm{c}_{\ell}\cdot[\bm{h}_{\ell,t}\ 1])\bm{d}_{\ell}, where [𝒉ℓ,t​ 1]∈ℝk+1[\bm{h}_{\ell,t}\ 1]\in\mathbb{R}^{k+1} is the concatenation of 𝒉ℓ,t∈ℝk\bm{h}_{\ell,t}\in\mathbb{R}^{k} with a constant 1, and 𝒅ℓ∈ℝk\bm{d}_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{k} is an extracted steering vector. To learn the sensing vector, we minimize the standard next-token prediction objective on a small dataset of prompt-completion pairs. This differs from tuning the coefficients in LAS, which uses an evaluator to select a fixed coefficient that produces the best generated outputs over a set of prompts.

We evaluate the effectiveness of our method on 11 diverse steering tasks using four instruction-tuned LLMs. In these tasks, the LLMs are steered to execute behaviors such as step-by-step reasoning, multilingual translation, tldr-style summarization, and other behaviors without explicit instruction and with only limited completion data for tuning. We compare our method against LAS and two popular parameter-efficient fine-tuning baselines, ReFT [37] and LoRA [18]. We find that our method outperforms LAS in nearly every model-task pair and is significantly faster to tune. We also find that CLAS matches or exceeds both ReFT and LoRA in these settings. We additionally evaluate whether the low-rank directions learned by ReFT and LoRA encode interpretable concepts by testing them as linear probes on 11 concept monitoring tasks. We find that they can be used for concept monitoring, but the probe-derived steering vectors used by CLAS consistently achieve much higher accuracy. Together, these results demonstrate that CLAS is a scalable and general extension of linear activation steering, retaining its interpretability while achieving high performance across many tasks.

Paper outline. In Section 2, we introduce our context-dependent activation steering method, CLAS, and describe its implementation for steering, including how to obtain the per-block steering and sensing vectors. In Section 3, we give an overview of the 11 steering tasks and their associated datasets, define the baselines, describe the experimental setup, and specify how we evaluate steering performance. In Section 4, we present results on the 11 steering tasks, which include steering and evaluating each task separately, as well as measuring how steering toward a single task interferes with performance on the other tasks. In Section 5, we evaluate how the probe-derived steering vectors used by CLAS and the low-rank directions learned by ReFT and LoRA perform on 11 concept monitoring tasks. In Section 6, we conclude with a brief summary.

2 Method

We describe our method in the context of steering LLMs using their internal activations. Although we focus on LLMs, our approach is generally applicable to any deep learning model. We first briefly outline the architecture of an LLM and then describe how to obtain the steering and sensing vectors for our method, CLAS.
